title: Perfect fluids in special relativity
one_line_summary: Builds the special-relativistic description of continuous matter step by step: dust and its number-flux four-vector, one-forms as the natural representation of surfaces, the stress-energy tensor read as a table of momentum fluxes, its symmetry, the local conservation laws (T^{ab}_{,b}=0, N^a_{,a}=0), the perfect-fluid tensor (rho+p)U(x)U + p g^{-1}, and from these the adiabatic condition and the relativistic Euler equation, closing with why T must be the source of gravity and with the four-dimensional Gauss theorem.
role_in_book: Chapter 3 supplied one-forms and general tensors as abstract machines; Chapter 4 gives them their first physical jobs before the book turns to curved manifolds in Chapters 5-6. It fixes the source side of GR: the stress-energy tensor, the perfect-fluid model, and the conservation law T^{ab}_{,b}=0 that Chapter 7 will rewrite with covariant derivatives and Chapter 8 will place on the right-hand side of Einstein's equations. It is also the first place the reader manipulates tensor-calculus expressions (derivatives of products, contraction with U, projection in the MCRF), and it previews the physics of relativistic stars (pressure as a source and as inertia, hence collapse; Chapters 10-11) and of cosmological fluids (Chapter 12). The MCRF-per-element idea introduced here is reused in Chapter 5 as the model for local inertial frames.

assumed_background.topic: Lorentz transformations, Lorentz contraction and the gamma factor (1-v^2)^{-1/2}
Four-velocity, four-momentum, rest mass as a scalar, and the momentarily comoving reference frame (MCRF)
assumed_background.where: SCH ch2 (MCRF in §2.3; E = -p.U in Eq. 2.35)

assumed_background.topic: One-forms as linear maps on vectors, gradient one-forms, (M N) tensors as multilinear machines, basis one-forms, the metric and index raising/lowering
Summation convention and comma notation for partial derivatives; the product rule applied to tensor components
Divergence theorem (Gauss' law) and flux integrals in three dimensions, e.g. for the electric field
Torque, moment of inertia, Newton's second law for a small body
Stress in continuous media, viscosity as shear stress, Euler equation and the advective derivative of fluid dynamics
First law of thermodynamics, heat, work p dV, temperature and entropy
Integrating factors for a differential expression in two variables
Baryons (protons, neutrons) and the idea of a conserved baryon number
Maxwell's equations in three-vector form (for Exercise 4.25 only)
Rough sense of astrophysical densities and pressures (ordinary stars versus neutron stars)

learning_objectives: Decide whether the continuum approximation applies to a system by asking whether elements exist that are large enough to average over yet small enough to be homogeneous.
Explain why a fluid is characterized by weak shear (anti-slip) forces and why a perfect fluid has none, leaving only pressure.
Derive the number density n/sqrt(1-v^2) and particle flux n v^i/sqrt(1-v^2) of dust in a frame where it moves, using Lorentz contraction of a box of particles.
Assemble density and fluxes into the number-flux four-vector N = nU and recover the rest density as the scalar n = (-N.N)^{1/2}.
Interpret a flux as world lines piercing a three-surface in spacetime, and see number density as the flux across a surface of constant t.
Represent a hypersurface by its (unit) normal one-form and compute the flux across it as the contraction <n~, N>; describe an inertial frame by the one-form dt and write E = <dt, p>.

Argue from counting one-forms (or gamma factors) that energy density must be a component of a (2 0) tensor, and state the component meaning of T^{ab} as the flux of a-momentum across a surface of constant x^b.
Show that dust has T = rho U(x)U and write its components in any frame.
Define the MCRF scalars of a fluid (n, rho, rho_0, Pi, T, p, S) and derive n dq = drho - (rho+p) dn/n = nT dS from the first law with particle conservation.
Interpret each block of T in the MCRF (energy density, heat flux, momentum density, stress) and prove T^{ab} = T^{ba} with the shrinking-cube torque argument.
Derive the local conservation laws T^{ab}_{,b} = 0 and N^a_{,a} = 0 by energy/particle bookkeeping on a small box.
Deduce the perfect-fluid tensor diag(rho,p,p,p) in the MCRF from 'no heat conduction, no viscosity', and promote it to T^{ab} = (rho+p)U^aU^b + p eta^{ab}.

Project the conservation law along U to obtain adiabatic flow (dS/dtau = 0) and perpendicular to U to obtain the relativistic Euler equation (rho+p)a_i + p_{,i} = 0, identifying rho+p as inertial mass density.
Explain qualitatively why the full T, including pressure, must source gravity and why this makes pressure support self-defeating in very compact stars.
State and apply the four-dimensional Gauss theorem with outward normal one-forms to turn the differential conservation laws into integral balance statements.

teaching_approach.summary: Schutz climbs a ladder of increasingly realistic matter models - dust, general single-component fluid, perfect fluid - and at every rung asks the same two questions: what is this quantity in the rest frame of the element, and what geometric object carries it into every other frame? Physical counting arguments (boxes of particles that Lorentz-contract, energy flowing through the faces of a small cube, torques on a shrinking element) come first; the one-form/vector/tensor language of Chapter 3 is then used to name what the counting found. Rank is diagnosed by how many one-forms a quantity needs (or how many gamma factors it picks up). A recurring device is to compute components in the MCRF, where everything is simple, and then write a frame-independent tensor equation that reduces to those components. The chapter ends by using the new tensor calculus on the perfect-fluid tensor, extracting thermodynamics and the Euler equation from one divergence, and by pointing forward to GR, where the whole of T must gravitate.
narrative_arc: Motivation: astrophysical sources of gravity are often well modelled as perfect fluids; set up the continuum idea (fields defined through averaging over elements, each with its own MCRF) and characterize fluids by weak shear forces.

Simplest model, dust: count particles in the rest frame (n), then boost and let the box Lorentz-contract, giving density n gamma; count the particles in a slanted box that reach a surface in time dt to get the flux n gamma v^i.

Unification: the four numbers are the components of one vector N = nU; the Galilean split into an invariant density and a frame-dependent flux vector is an artefact of looking at three of four components; n = sqrt(-N.N) is a scalar like rest mass.

Geometric reinterpretation: a flux is the number of world lines crossing a unit three-volume of a hypersurface; choosing the hypersurface t = const shows density is a timelike flux; hypersurfaces are best described by normal one-forms, and the flux is <n~, N>. Bonus: a frame is naturally described by dt, with E = <dt, p>.

Energy and momentum of dust: energy density picks up two gamma factors, so it cannot be a vector component; count the one-forms needed and define T by its component meaning; build T = p(x)N = rho U(x)U from its MCRF values and check the moving-frame components against first principles.

General fluids: define all scalars in the element's MCRF (Table 4.1); use the first law and particle number conservation to reach n dq = drho - (rho+p)dn/n, and define T and S through an integrating factor.

Read T in the MCRF block by block (energy density, heat-conduction energy flux, associated momentum density, stress) and show stresses are the forces between neighbouring elements; prove symmetry of T^{ij} with a torque argument on a vanishing cube and equality of energy flux and momentum density from E = m.

Conservation: balance energy flowing through the six faces of a small cube against the rate of change inside and shrink the cube to reach T^{0b}_{,b} = 0, then T^{ab}_{,b} = 0; do the same for particles, N^a_{,a} = 0, justified by baryon conservation.

Perfect fluid: no heat conduction kills T^{0i}; no viscosity forces T^{ij} diagonal in every rotated frame, hence p delta^{ij}; write diag(rho,p,p,p), verify that (rho+p)U^aU^b + p eta^{ab} reproduces it, and promote to a tensor equation. Dust is the p = 0 case; pressure comes from random motion even without collisions.

First tensor-calculus workout: expand the divergence using particle conservation and U^a_{,b}U_a = 0; the component along U gives drho/dtau = (rho+p)/n dn/dtau, i.e. dS/dtau = 0 (adiabatic flow); the components orthogonal to U, evaluated in the MCRF, give (rho+p)a_i + p_{,i} = 0, the relativistic Euler equation with inertia rho+p.

Look ahead to GR: a relativistic source cannot be rest-mass density or T^{00} alone, so Einstein took all of T; pressure both gravitates and adds inertia, so in very compact stars raising pressure fails and collapse follows; p approaches rho only in neutron-star matter or ultra-hot gases.

Integral form: state the four-dimensional Gauss theorem, evaluate it on a coordinate box with outward normal one-forms (+-dt, +-dx), and read it as particle or energy bookkeeping; the exercises extend the machinery to collisionless gases, the virial theorem, radiation from a moving star and the Faraday tensor.
signature_moves: Rest-frame first, then promote: find components in the MCRF where the physics is transparent, then exhibit a tensor expression that reproduces them, concluding it holds in all frames (dust T, perfect-fluid T, symmetry of T proven in one frame).

Rank by counting: a number density needs one one-form (the surface) and picks up one gamma; energy density needs two one-forms (which component of momentum, which surface) and picks up two gammas, so it is a component of a (2 0) tensor.
Spacetime flux picture: surfaces become world-tubes, particles become world lines, and 'density' is just the flux across the t = const slice, which unifies density and flux before any algebra.

Explicit parallel with 3D electrostatics: the flux E.n of Gauss' law becomes the contraction of N with the unit normal one-form, keeping properties of the matter (N) separate from properties of the surface (n~).
Shrinking-element limits used as reductio: unbalanced forces or asymmetric stresses would give a vanishing element infinite linear or angular acceleration.
Newtonian checkpoints: Euler equation, continuity equation, advective derivative and Newton's second law are recovered as limits (in text and in Exercises 4.9, 4.10, 4.17, 4.18).

Thermodynamics as a by-product of conservation: temperature and entropy enter only as an integrating factor of the first law, and entropy conservation later drops out of the U-component of T^{ab}_{,b}=0.
Deliberate forward-looking physics payoff: the chapter closes its SR material by arguing, without equations, why pressure matters more in GR and leads to collapse.

sections.title: Fluids
sections.summary: Motivates fluids as first-approximation sources in astrophysical GR, defines a continuum as matter described only by averaged fields, introduces the fluid element (big enough to average, small enough to be uniform) with its own MCRF, and separates fluids from solids by the strength of forces tangent to the interface between elements; a perfect fluid has no such forces, only pressure.
key_moves: Gravity of a lake depends on bulk averages, not on individual molecules, motivating field variables.
Element size is squeezed between graininess and inhomogeneity; if no such scale exists (very rarefied gas) the continuum picture fails.
Rigidity is traced to shear forces that stop neighbouring elements sliding; weakness of these defines a fluid, their absence a perfect fluid.

sections.title: Dust: the number-flux vector N
sections.summary: Defines dust as particles sharing a common rest frame, defines the scalar n as the rest-frame number density, derives the moving-frame density (one gamma factor from Lorentz contraction) and the flux across constant-x surfaces from a box of particles, and shows these are the components of N = nU; stresses that this unifies Galilean density and flux into a single frame-independent vector, with n = sqrt(-N.N).
key_moves: Lorentz contraction along the motion shrinks the volume by sqrt(1-v^2), raising the density to n/sqrt(1-v^2) (Eq. 4.2).
Particles that cross area dA in time dt fill a box of length v dt; with a general velocity the box is a parallelepiped whose height is v^x dt, giving Eq. 4.3.
N = nU has components (n gamma, n gamma v^i): time component = density, space components = fluxes (Eq. 4.5).
Frame independence refers to the geometric object, not the components; the old 3-flux was frame dependent because it was only three of four components.
N.N = -n^2 makes n a scalar, the analogue of rest mass (Eq. 4.6).

sections.title: One-forms and surfaces
sections.summary: Redraws the flux calculation in a spacetime diagram, where a spatial surface sweeps out a three-dimensional world-tube and flux is the count of world lines through a unit three-volume of it; choosing a t = const slice shows density is a timelike flux. Surfaces phi = const are then represented by the gradient one-form or the unit normal one-form, and flux becomes <n~, N>. Finally an inertial frame is characterized by dt (its surfaces of simultaneity), giving E = <dt, p> without the minus sign of E = -p.U.
concepts: flux as contraction of one-form with vector
key_moves: Flux across a constant-x surface = world lines crossing a unit cube dt dy dz of the surface's world-tube (Fig. 4.4).
Replacing the world-tube by a slice t = const, the same count is the number in a unit spatial volume: density (Fig. 4.5).
Normal one-form d phi fixes the surface up to scale; normalize by |d phi| = |eta^{ab} phi_{,a} phi_{,b}|^{1/2} when the surface is not null (Eqs. 4.7-4.8).
Check with phi = x: <dx, N> = N^x, the flux; phi = t gives N^0, the density.
The frame one-form g(U, .) equals -dt, so dt (surfaces of simultaneity) specifies the frame and E = <dt, p> = p^0 (Eq. 4.10).

sections.title: Dust again: the stress-energy tensor
sections.summary: Introduces rho as MCRF energy density (rho = mn for dust), shows that the moving-frame energy density rho/(1-v^2) has two gamma factors, and argues that energy density, energy flux, momentum density and momentum flux each need two one-forms, so they are components of a (2 0) tensor T. Defines T^{ab} as the flux of a-momentum across constant-x^b surfaces, interprets the four blocks, and identifies dust's T as p(x)N = rho U(x)U, whose boosted components match first-principles expectations and are symmetric.
key_moves: Energy per particle and number per volume each gain gamma: rho/(1-v^2) (Eq. 4.13), impossible for a vector component.
One one-form selects the energy (or momentum) component, the other selects the surface: two slots, a (2 0) tensor.
Component definition T(dx^a, dx^b) = T^{ab} (Eq. 4.14) with block meanings (Eqs. 4.15-4.18); linearity proof deferred to Exercise 4.5.
In the MCRF dust has only T^{00} = rho; p(x)N has the same components, so T = rho U(x)U (Eq. 4.19) and T^{ab} = rho U^aU^b (Eq. 4.20).
Moving-frame components (Eq. 4.21) are symmetric, foreshadowing a general result.

sections.title: General fluids
sections.summary: Adds random particle motions and interparticle forces. All fluid scalars are defined in the (element- and time-dependent) MCRF, collected in Table 4.1. The first law with a fixed particle number gives n dq = drho - (rho+p)dn/n, whose integrating factor defines temperature and specific entropy. The MCRF blocks of T are interpreted (heat conduction appears in T^{0i}), T^{ij} is shown to be the force per area between adjacent elements, and T is proven symmetric: T^{ij} by a torque argument on a shrinking cube, T^{0i} = T^{i0} because moving energy is moving mass.
concepts: first law of thermodynamics for a fluid element
temperature and specific entropy via integrating factor
equality of energy flux and momentum density
key_moves: MCRF is local in space and time; every fluid scalar is its MCRF value (Table 4.1: U, n, N, rho, Pi, rho_0, T, p, S).
dQ = dE + p dV with V = N/n and E = rho N/n gives n dq = drho - (rho+p) dn/n (Eqs. 4.22-4.24).
A two-variable differential form always has an integrating factor: drho - (rho+p)dn/n = nT dS, so dq = T dS (Eqs. 4.25-4.26).
Force F from element A on B across area A pours momentum at rate F: T^{ij} = F^i/A; forces normal to faces give a diagonal T^{ij}.
Torque on a cube of side l is l^3(T^{xy} - T^{yx}) while inertia scales as l^5; angular acceleration would diverge as l -> 0 unless T^{xy} = T^{yx} (Eqs. 4.27-4.29).
Energy flux = energy density x speed = mass density x speed = momentum density, so T^{0i} = T^{i0}.

sections.title: Conservation of energy-momentum
sections.summary: Balances the energy flowing across the faces of a small cubical element against the rate of change of energy inside; dividing by the volume and shrinking the cube yields the four-divergence law T^{0b}_{,b} = 0, and by the same reasoning T^{ab}_{,b} = 0 for momentum, valid for any material in SR. The same argument for particles gives N^a_{,a} = (nU^a)_{,a} = 0, which the book assumes throughout by taking n to count baryons.
key_moves: Inflow through face at x = 0 minus outflow at x = l, for all three directions, equals d(l^3 T^{00})/dt (Eq. 4.30).
Limit l -> 0 converts differences to derivatives (Eqs. 4.31-4.32), giving T^{0a}_{,a} = 0 (Eq. 4.33).
Replacing the energy index by a momentum index gives T^{ab}_{,b} = 0 (Eq. 4.34).
Particle bookkeeping gives N^a_{,a} = 0 (Eq. 4.35); baryon number makes this almost no restriction.

sections.title: Perfect fluids
sections.summary: Defines a perfect fluid as having no viscosity and no heat conduction in the MCRF. These kill T^{0i} and force T^{ij} to be diagonal in every rotated MCRF, hence proportional to delta^{ij}, the proportionality constant being the pressure. The MCRF matrix diag(rho,p,p,p) is matched by (rho+p)U^aU^b + p eta^{ab} and promoted to T = (rho+p)U(x)U + p g^{-1}. Dust is the pressureless case and pressure is momentum flux from random motion. Expanding T^{ab}_{,b} = 0 with particle conservation and U^a_{,b}U_a = 0 gives, along U, conservation of specific entropy, and orthogonal to U, the relativistic Euler equation (rho+p)a_i + p_{,i} = 0.
concepts: pressure as momentum flux from random motion
orthogonality of four-velocity and its gradient
key_moves: No heat conduction: energy moves only with particles, so T^{0i} = T^{i0} = 0 in the MCRF.
No viscosity: T^{ij} diagonal for all orientations of the spatial axes, so T^{ij} = p delta^{ij}; six functions reduce to one.
Matrix (Eq. 4.36) reproduced by (rho+p)U^aU^b + p eta^{ab} (Eq. 4.37), hence the tensor Eq. 4.38.
Pressure-free perfect fluid = dust; a collisionless gas still has pressure because pressure is momentum flux.
Differentiate U^aU_a = -1 to get U^a_{,b}U_a = 0 (Eqs. 4.42-4.44).
Contract Eq. 4.45 with U_a: U^b[rho_{,b} - (rho+p)n_{,b}/n] = 0, i.e. drho/dtau = (rho+p)/n dn/dtau, which with Eq. 4.25 means dS/dtau = 0 (Eqs. 4.46-4.50).
In the MCRF U^i = 0 but its derivatives are not zero; the spatial components give (rho+p)U_{i,b}U^b + p_{,i} = 0, i.e. (rho+p)a_i + p_{,i} = 0 (Eqs. 4.51-4.54).
Compare to the Newtonian rho a + grad p = 0: rho+p is the inertial mass density, and only a pressure difference across the element pushes it.

sections.title: Importance for general relativity
sections.summary: Looks ahead: a relativistic theory cannot use rest-mass density as its gravitational source (mass and energy interconvert, and precision experiments rule it out), nor T^{00} alone (frame dependent), so Einstein took the whole tensor T. Pressure therefore both sources gravity and contributes inertia via rho+p. In a compact star the pressure gradient needed to resist gravity is larger than in Newtonian theory and itself adds to gravity; once p is comparable with rho, no pressure suffices and collapse is inevitable. p ~ rho only in neutron-star matter or relativistic gases.
concepts: stress-energy tensor as source of gravity
pressure as a source of gravity
key_moves: Rule out rest-mass density (not relativistic, conflicts with experiment) and T^{00} alone (needs a preferred frame); only the full tensor is acceptable.
Hydrostatic support: required pressure gradient p_{,i} = -(rho+p) a_i exceeds the Newtonian value.
Feedback loop: extra pressure is extra source, requiring more pressure; for p comparable to rho this runs away into collapse.

sections.title: Gauss' law
sections.summary: States the four-dimensional divergence theorem relating the four-volume integral of V^a_{,a} to the flux of V through the bounding three-surface with outward unit normal one-forms, and evaluates the surface term on a coordinate box: the t = const faces carry +-V^0, the x = const faces carry +-V^x. For N or T^{0a} this reads as 'change in the amount inside equals net flow across the walls', the integral version of particle and energy conservation.
concepts: outward normal orientation on spacetime boundaries
key_moves: Proof taken over from 3D without detail (Eq. 4.57).
Outward normals on a box: dt on the later face, -dt on the earlier face (outward = to the past), +-dx on the spatial faces (Fig. 4.9).
Surface integral becomes differences of V^0 between times plus differences of V^x between walls (Eq. 4.58); with divergence zero, content change equals boundary flux.

sections.title: Bibliography
sections.summary: Points readers weak in thermodynamics or fluid mechanics to Fermi and to Landau & Lifshitz, to Landau & Lifshitz and Jackson for the electromagnetic stress-energy tensor, to Israel & Stewart for dissipative relativistic fluids, and to Andreasson for collisionless (kinetic) matter in GR.
key_moves: Signals that viscosity and heat flow in relativity are subtle and deferred to specialist literature.
Offers kinetic theory as an alternative continuum model to fluids.

concepts.name: continuum approximation
concepts.definition: Treating a system of enormously many particles through smooth fields (density, velocity, pressure, temperature, ...) defined at every event, obtained by averaging over elements; valid only when a scale exists that is large compared with interparticle spacing yet small compared with the scale on which averages vary.
concepts.how_introduced: Opens the chapter: the gravity of a lake depends on averaged properties, not on which molecule is where; the need for an averaging scale is derived from the fact that averages vary with depth or altitude.
concepts.notes: Exercise 4.1 asks the reader to test the approximation on planets, lava, traffic and plasmas.

concepts.name: fluid element
concepts.definition: A collection of particles large enough that individual particles are irrelevant but small enough that density, mean velocity, temperature etc. can be taken as single values; in the continuum limit it is idealized as a point.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined as the answer to 'how big a region should one average over?'; admitted to be an imprecise but useful term.

concepts.name: momentarily comoving reference frame
aliases: rest frame of a fluid element
concepts.definition: For a given fluid element at a given event, the inertial frame in which the element's total spatial momentum is zero at that instant; it varies from element to element and from moment to moment because elements accelerate and move relative to each other.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled from particle kinematics (§2.3) and assigned to each fluid element; later stressed that it is truly momentary and local, and used as the frame in which all fluid scalars are defined and all component calculations are done.
concepts.notes: Chapter 5 reuses this idea as the analogy for local inertial frames in curved spacetime.

concepts.name: fluid
concepts.definition: A continuum in which the forces between neighbouring elements that act parallel to their common interface (shear or anti-slip forces) are weak compared with the normal push-pull force (pressure), so the material flows.
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted with rigid solids by asking what makes a substance rigid; the answer is tangential forces that stop elements sliding. The boundary is acknowledged to be fuzzy since most solids flow under high pressure.

concepts.name: perfect fluid
concepts.definition: A fluid with no viscosity and no heat conduction in the MCRF of each element, so that the only interaction between neighbouring elements is isotropic pressure; its stress-energy tensor is fully fixed by rho, p and U.
concepts.how_introduced: Previewed in §4.1 as a fluid with zero anti-slip forces; defined precisely in §4.7 by the two MCRF conditions, and called a relativistic generalization of the ideal gas and, after dust, the simplest fluid.

concepts.name: dust
concepts.definition: A collection of particles with no random motions: at each event all nearby particles share one velocity, so in the MCRF every particle is at rest; it has zero pressure and T = rho U(x)U.
concepts.how_introduced: Chosen as the simplest possible fluid to launch the relativistic description; the book jokes about the name. Later identified as the p = 0 case of the perfect fluid.
concepts.notes: The book's first definition says all particles are at rest in 'some Lorentz frame'; for a general flow this should be read element by element.

concepts.name: number density
concepts.definition: The scalar n equal to the number of particles per unit volume measured in the element's MCRF; in a frame where the particles move with speed v the measured number per unit volume is larger, n/sqrt(1-v^2).
concepts.how_introduced: Found by counting particles in a box in the rest frame, then noting that in a moving frame the same particles occupy a Lorentz-contracted box (Fig. 4.1).

concepts.name: particle flux
concepts.definition: The number of particles crossing unit area of a given surface per unit time; it depends on both the frame (through area and time) and the orientation of the surface, and for dust across a constant-x surface equals n v^x/sqrt(1-v^2).
concepts.how_introduced: Computed by drawing the box (or slanted parallelepiped) of particles that will reach the surface within a time interval (Figs. 4.2-4.3).
concepts.notes: Exercise 4.2 criticizes the loose phrase 'flux in the x direction': the flux is across a surface of constant x.

concepts.name: number-flux four-vector
concepts.definition: The four-vector N = nU whose component along the one-form dt in any frame is the particle density there and whose components along dx^i are the particle fluxes across surfaces of constant x^i.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by noticing that the density and fluxes of dust computed separately are exactly n times the components of the four-velocity; celebrated as a unification of Galilean density and flux.

concepts.name: geometric object versus components
concepts.definition: A vector or tensor exists independently of any frame and gives frame-independent numbers when fed frame-independent arguments, while its components, being its values on a particular basis, change from frame to frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Re-emphasized from Chapter 3 using N: the prerelativistic 3-flux was frame dependent because it was only three of the four components of a single invariant object.

concepts.name: rest-frame scalar quantities
concepts.definition: The rule that every scalar attribute of a fluid element (number density, energy density, pressure, temperature, specific entropy, ...) is defined as its value measured in that element's MCRF, which makes it a Lorentz scalar.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the analogy between n and rest mass, then stated as a blanket convention for general fluids and tabulated in Table 4.1.
concepts.notes: The book limits itself to single-component fluids (one species of particle), so interpenetrating flows with several four-velocities at one event are excluded.

concepts.name: number density as timelike flux
aliases: density as flux across t = const
concepts.definition: Number density in a frame is the flux of particle world lines across a hypersurface of constant time in that frame, just as spatial fluxes are world-line crossings of hypersurfaces of constant x^i.
concepts.how_introduced: Shown with a pair of spacetime diagrams: first world lines crossing the world-tube of a surface x = const in an interval dt, then the same world lines crossing a slice t = const across an interval dx.

concepts.name: hypersurface
concepts.definition: A three-dimensional surface in four-dimensional spacetime, typically a level set phi(t,x,y,z) = const; a two-dimensional spatial surface at rest sweeps out such a three-surface over time, and a surface of simultaneity is another example.
concepts.how_introduced: Arises when the spatial surface of the flux calculation is followed through time in a spacetime diagram; its 'unit volume' is dt dy dz.

concepts.name: normal one-form
concepts.definition: For a hypersurface phi = const, the gradient one-form d phi (components phi_{,a}); it vanishes on every vector tangent to the surface and so determines the surface, but only up to an overall factor.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as a cleaner representation of surfaces than the 'clumsy' description via world-tubes.

concepts.name: unit normal one-form
concepts.definition: The normal one-form rescaled to unit magnitude using the inverse metric, n~ = d phi/|d phi| with |d phi| = |eta^{ab} phi_{,a} phi_{,b}|^{1/2}; defined only for non-null hypersurfaces.
concepts.how_introduced: Presented in direct analogy with the unit normal of 3D vector calculus, and later used with an outward sense in the 4D Gauss theorem.
concepts.notes: The book warns that n~ has nothing to do with the number density n despite the shared letter.

concepts.name: hypersurface volume element
concepts.definition: The directed three-volume element of a hypersurface, formed as the unit normal one-form times the coordinate three-volume dx^a dx^b dx^c spanning the surface; a unit three-volume is represented by n~ itself.
concepts.how_introduced: Generalized from the vector area element (unit normal times area) of 3D Gauss' law.

concepts.name: flux as contraction of one-form with vector
concepts.definition: The flux of a conserved current N across a hypersurface is the number obtained by contracting N with the surface's unit normal one-form, <n~, N> = N^a n_a; the matter and the surface enter as separate objects.
concepts.how_introduced: Compared with E.n in electrostatics; checked by choosing phi = x (giving N^x) and phi = t (giving N^0, the density). Presented as a physical instance of a vector being a function of one-forms.

concepts.name: frame as a one-form
aliases: dt as a family of simultaneity surfaces
concepts.definition: An inertial frame can be specified by the one-form dt, pictured as its stack of surfaces of simultaneity, instead of by its four-velocity; the two are related by g(U, .) = -dt, and energy in the frame is E = <dt, p> = p^0.
concepts.how_introduced: Offered as a 'useful fact' after the surface discussion: lowering the frame's U gives components (-1,0,0,0), identical to -dt.

concepts.name: energy density
concepts.definition: The scalar rho equal to the total energy per unit volume (rest mass plus random kinetic, chemical, interaction energies) measured in the MCRF; for dust rho = mn.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced for dust by multiplying particle energy m by number density n in the rest frame; broadened in Table 4.1 to all forms of energy.

concepts.name: gamma-squared transformation of energy density
concepts.definition: Energy per unit volume of dust seen in a frame where it moves is rho/(1-v^2): one gamma from the increased energy per particle and one from Lorentz contraction of the volume, which shows energy density is not a component of a four-vector.
concepts.how_introduced: Computed directly after the energy density is defined, then used as the key clue that a second-rank tensor is needed.

concepts.name: stress-energy tensor
concepts.definition: The symmetric (2 0) tensor T whose component T^{ab} = T(dx^a, dx^b) in any inertial frame is the flux of the a-component of four-momentum across a surface of constant x^b: T^{00} energy density, T^{0i} energy flux, T^{i0} momentum density, T^{ij} momentum flux (stress).
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by counting one-forms: selecting 'energy' (a component of p) needs one, selecting 'density' or 'flux across a surface' needs another. Defined via components in an arbitrary frame, with tensor character left to Exercise 4.5.

concepts.name: dust stress-energy tensor
concepts.definition: For dust of particle rest mass m, T = p(x)N = mn U(x)U = rho U(x)U, with components rho U^aU^b in any frame: rho gamma^2 energy density, rho gamma^2 v^i energy flux and momentum density, rho gamma^2 v^iv^j momentum flux.
concepts.how_introduced: Only T^{00} = rho is non-zero in the MCRF; the outer product p(x)N has exactly that component pattern there, so the two tensors are equal.

concepts.name: rest-mass density
concepts.definition: rho_0 = mn, the energy associated with the rest mass of the particles alone per unit MCRF volume; it differs from rho by the internal energy density n Pi.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed in Table 4.1; used in §4.8 as the quantity closest to Newton's gravitational source, which a relativistic theory must replace.

concepts.name: internal energy per particle
concepts.definition: Pi = rho/n - m, the energy per particle over and above its rest mass (thermal kinetic, chemical, interaction), so that rho = n(m + Pi).
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in Table 4.1 as a catch-all for non-rest-mass energies.

concepts.name: two-parameter thermodynamic state
concepts.definition: For a simple single-component fluid in local equilibrium, all thermodynamic quantities (p, T, S, ...) are functions of any two independent ones, e.g. rho and n.
concepts.how_introduced: Asserted without proof ('it can be shown') to justify treating drho - (rho+p)dn/n as a differential form in two variables.

concepts.name: first law of thermodynamics for a fluid element
concepts.definition: Energy conservation for a fluid element in its MCRF: heat absorbed equals increase in energy plus work p dV; with a fixed number of particles this becomes n dq = drho - (rho+p) dn/n, q being heat per particle.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived using V = N/n and E = rho V to eliminate the volume, explicitly as a statement of energy conservation in the MCRF.

concepts.name: temperature and specific entropy via integrating factor
concepts.definition: Because drho - (rho+p)dn/n is a differential form in two variables it admits an integrating factor: it equals A dB, and one defines temperature T = A/n and specific entropy S = B, giving drho - (rho+p)dn/n = nT dS and dq = T dS.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced as a mathematical convenience flowing from the first law, with the assurance (not proved) that T and S coincide with thermodynamic temperature and the entropy of the second law.
prerequisites: first law of thermodynamics for a fluid element
concepts.notes: Exercise 4.8 shows that the heat one-form is not exact: there is no function q whose gradient it is.

concepts.name: heat conduction
concepts.definition: Transport of energy without bulk motion of the fluid; in the MCRF it appears as non-zero T^{0i}, and because moving energy carries momentum, as non-zero T^{i0}.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from the block structure of T in the MCRF; its absence is one of the two defining conditions of a perfect fluid.

concepts.name: stress
concepts.definition: The spatial block T^{ij} of the stress-energy tensor: the flux of i-momentum across a surface of constant x^j, equivalently the i-component of force per unit area that the material on one side exerts on the other across that surface.
concepts.how_introduced: Interpreted using two adjacent cubical elements (Fig. 4.6): a force F across the shared face transfers momentum at rate F, so the momentum flux is F/A. Forces normal to faces give diagonal stresses; tangential ones (viscosity, rigidity) give off-diagonal stresses. Newton's second law can be used here because in the MCRF the velocities vanish; the force from A pours momentum into B whether or not B ends up accelerating, since B's net motion depends on all its neighbours.
concepts.notes: In Newtonian physics T^{ij} is the familiar engineering stress tensor, which gives T its name.

concepts.name: symmetry of the stress-energy tensor
concepts.definition: The stress-energy tensor is symmetric, T(q~, r~) = T(r~, q~); in the MCRF this splits into T^{ij} = T^{ji} (from finite angular acceleration of small elements) and T^{0i} = T^{i0} (energy flux equals momentum density).
concepts.how_introduced: First noticed in the dust components (Eq. 4.21), then proved for any material by showing symmetry of components in one frame (the MCRF), which implies symmetry of the tensor and so of its components in every frame.

concepts.name: equality of energy flux and momentum density
concepts.definition: In relativity (c = 1) energy and inertial mass are the same thing, so the rate at which energy flows through unit area equals the density of momentum carried: T^{0i} = T^{i0}.
concepts.how_introduced: A two-line physical argument following the torque proof.

concepts.name: local conservation of energy-momentum
concepts.definition: In special relativity the energy and momentum of any closed material system satisfy T^{ab}_{,b} = 0: in each frame the time rate of change of the density of a-momentum is balanced by the divergence of its flux.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by energy bookkeeping on a small cube (Fig. 4.8) with inflow and outflow through opposite faces, followed by the limit l -> 0; momentum components follow by relabelling the index.
concepts.notes: Exercise 4.20 shows how an external four-force appears as a source, and Exercise 4.9 recovers Newton's second law from the spatial components.

concepts.name: four-divergence
concepts.definition: The contraction V^a_{,a} = dV^0/dt + dV^x/dx + dV^y/dy + dV^z/dz of the gradient of a vector field with itself; a frame-independent scalar in SR.
concepts.how_introduced: Recognized in the conservation laws ('just a four-dimensional divergence').

concepts.name: conservation of particle number
concepts.definition: If particles are neither created nor destroyed, the number-flux vector is divergence free, (nU^a)_{,a} = 0; in the Newtonian limit this is dn/dt + div(n v) = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived by the same box argument as energy conservation, then assumed for all fluids in the book.

concepts.name: baryon number conservation
concepts.definition: The total number of baryons (protons, neutrons and heavier unstable relatives that decay into them) is conserved in all observed processes, even when rest mass and particle identity change, so n can always be taken as baryon density.
concepts.how_introduced: A reassuring aside explaining why particle conservation is hardly a restriction; notes theoretical exceptions (grand unified proton decay, black-hole formation and evaporation) that are unobserved or irrelevant for most problems.

concepts.name: viscosity
concepts.definition: Forces between neighbouring fluid elements acting parallel to their common interface; they appear as off-diagonal spatial stresses T^{ij} (i != j).
concepts.how_introduced: Identified with the 'anti-slipping' forces of §4.1; its absence is one of the two perfect-fluid conditions.

concepts.name: pressure
concepts.definition: The scalar p measured in the MCRF such that, when stresses are isotropic, the force per unit area across any surface is p along the surface normal: T^{ij} = p delta^{ij} in the MCRF.
concepts.how_introduced: Named in §4.1 as the normal push-pull force; defined precisely in §4.7: absence of viscosity makes T^{ij} diagonal for every rotation of axes, and only multiples of the identity have that property.

concepts.name: pressure as momentum flux from random motion
concepts.definition: Pressure is the flux of momentum across a surface in the MCRF, whether carried by forces between particles or by particles themselves crossing the surface; hence any matter with random velocities has pressure, even a collisionless gas, and only matter with no random motion (dust) is pressureless.
concepts.how_introduced: Brief 'aside on the meaning of pressure' drawn from comparing the perfect-fluid and dust tensors; made quantitative in Exercise 4.22.

concepts.name: perfect-fluid stress-energy tensor
concepts.definition: T = (rho+p) U(x)U + p g^{-1}, with components (rho+p)U^aU^b + p eta^{ab}; in the MCRF it is diag(rho, p, p, p).
concepts.how_introduced: The MCRF matrix is derived from the perfect-fluid conditions; a covariant expression is guessed and checked component by component (e.g. the 00 entry gives rho+p-p = rho) and then declared frame invariant.

concepts.name: orthogonality of four-velocity and its gradient
concepts.definition: Because U^aU_a = -1 everywhere, differentiating gives U_a U^a_{,b} = 0: the change of the four-velocity in any direction is orthogonal to the four-velocity itself.
concepts.how_introduced: Proved as a lemma needed for the perfect-fluid equations, using that eta is constant and symmetric (Eqs. 4.42-4.44).

concepts.name: derivative along a world line
concepts.definition: For a field f, the rate of change following a fluid element is df/dtau = U^b f_{,b}, the directional derivative along the four-velocity.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked as already known when the term p_{,b}U^b appears in the U-projection of the conservation law.

concepts.name: adiabatic flow
concepts.definition: In a particle-conserving perfect fluid each element keeps its specific entropy, U^aS_{,a} = dS/dtau = 0, because no heat is conducted.
concepts.how_introduced: Emerges from contracting the divergence of the perfect-fluid tensor with U_a: the result drho/dtau = (rho+p)/n dn/dtau is compared with the first law nT dS = drho - (rho+p)dn/n.
prerequisites: temperature and specific entropy via integrating factor
orthogonality of four-velocity and its gradient
concepts.notes: The book stresses that thermodynamic energy conservation is the component of T^{ab}_{,b}=0 parallel to U.

concepts.name: four-acceleration
concepts.definition: a^m = U^m_{,b}U^b = dU^m/dtau, the rate of change of four-velocity along the world line; orthogonal to U, so in the MCRF it has only spatial components.
concepts.how_introduced: Recalled as a definition when the spatial part of the fluid equation produces U_{i,b}U^b; Exercise 4.17 shows it reduces to the advective derivative Dv/Dt.

concepts.name: relativistic Euler equation
aliases: relativistic equation of motion of a perfect fluid
concepts.definition: The components of T^{ab}_{,b} = 0 orthogonal to U for a perfect fluid, which in the MCRF read (rho+p)a_i + p_{,i} = 0: the pressure gradient accelerates the element, resisted by the inertia rho+p.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by evaluating the spatial components of the expanded conservation law in the MCRF, where U^i = 0 but its derivatives need not vanish, then compared with the Newtonian rho a + grad p = 0.
concepts.notes: Exercise 4.18 asks for a sharper proof that -grad p is the net force per unit volume.

concepts.name: inertial mass density rho + p
concepts.definition: In relativistic fluid dynamics the combination rho + p, not rho, measures resistance of a fluid element to acceleration by pressure gradients; pressure contributes to inertia.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from the relativistic Euler equation by analogy with F = ma, then used in §4.8 to argue that relativistic stars need larger pressure gradients.
concepts.notes: Standard texts call rho+p the enthalpy density; Schutz does not use that name.

concepts.name: stress-energy tensor as source of gravity
concepts.definition: In GR the gravitational field is sourced by the whole stress-energy tensor, not by rest-mass density or energy density alone: every component, including momenta and stresses, gravitates.
concepts.how_introduced: Argued by elimination: rest mass is not invariantly separable from other energy and a rest-mass source conflicts with precision experiments; T^{00} alone would single out a frame; so Einstein chose T.

concepts.name: pressure as a source of gravity
concepts.definition: Because all of T sources gravity, pressure adds to the gravitational pull of matter; this, together with pressure's contribution to inertia, makes pressure more important in GR than in Newtonian theory.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated in §4.8 as the second key lesson of fluids for GR.
prerequisites: stress-energy tensor as source of gravity

concepts.name: relativistic gravitational collapse
concepts.definition: In sufficiently compact stars the extra pressure needed to support the star itself strengthens gravity and raises the required pressure further; once p is comparable with rho no pressure gradient can hold the star up and it must collapse.
concepts.how_introduced: Qualitative feedback argument using -a_i = p_{,i}/(rho+p) and pressure as a source; details deferred to later chapters.
prerequisites: pressure as a source of gravity
concepts.notes: Treat the book's 'p comparable with rho' as a heuristic. The sharp statement in GR is a bound on compactness: for static stars 2M/R < 8/9 (Buchdahl), from the TOV equation of Chapter 10. It is not a local threshold on p/rho.

concepts.name: Gauss' law in four dimensions
concepts.definition: For a vector field V on a four-volume with closed boundary, the integral of V^a_{,a} d^4x equals the integral over the boundary three-surface of V^a n_a d^3S, where n~ is the outward unit normal one-form; for a divergence-free V the net flux out of any closed hypersurface vanishes.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated without proof by appeal to the 3D theorem, then made concrete on a coordinate box (Fig. 4.9), turning N^a_{,a} = 0 and T^{0a}_{,a} = 0 into integral balance laws.
concepts.notes: Exercise 4.19 asks for the proof via Eq. 4.58; Exercise 4.25(g) uses it to recover the electric Gauss law.

concepts.name: outward normal orientation on spacetime boundaries
concepts.definition: On the boundary of a four-volume the unit normal one-form in Gauss' law is taken to point outward: dt on the later constant-time face, -dt on the earlier face (outward there means toward the past), dx on the larger-x face and -dx on the smaller-x face.
concepts.how_introduced: Spelled out for the box of Fig. 4.9 while evaluating the surface integral.

concepts.name: collisionless gas
concepts.definition: A system of particles that do not collide (e.g. radiation, rarefied plasma, stars in a galaxy or cluster) treated statistically; if its velocity distribution is isotropic in the MCRF its stress-energy tensor has perfect-fluid form, with pressure from particle motions.
concepts.how_introduced: Mentioned in the pressure aside and bibliography (Andreasson); worked out in Exercise 4.22, including p = rho/3 for photons.
prerequisites: pressure as momentum flux from random motion

concepts.name: dissipative relativistic fluids
concepts.definition: Relativistic fluids with viscosity and heat conduction, whose consistent (causal, stable) description is subtle and requires theories beyond the perfect fluid.
concepts.how_introduced: Only flagged in the bibliography, with a pointer to Israel & Stewart.

concepts.name: Faraday tensor
concepts.definition: The antisymmetric (2 0) tensor F with F^{0i} = E^i and F^{xy} = B^z (cyclic); Maxwell's equations become F^{mn}_{,n} = 4 pi J^m and F_{[mn,l]} = 0, and E and B mix under boosts as components of F.
concepts.how_introduced: Built step by step in the long Exercise 4.25, which also connects charge conservation and Gauss' law to the chapter's number-flux and integral-conservation ideas.

concepts.name: tensor virial theorem
concepts.definition: For a bounded system obeying T^{mn}_{,n} = 0, the second time derivative of the second moment of the energy distribution equals twice the volume integral of the stresses.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears only as Exercise 4.23(b), derived by repeatedly using the conservation law and integrating by parts.
concepts.notes: Reused later in the book's treatment of gravitational-wave generation (quadrupole formula).

key_equations.name: Rest number density
key_equations.latex: n := \text{number density in the MCRF of the element}
key_equations.meaning: n is always the count per unit volume in the element's own rest frame, hence a scalar.

key_equations.name: Number density in a moving frame
key_equations.latex: \frac{n}{\sqrt{1-v^2}} = \text{number density where the particles move with speed } v
key_equations.meaning: Lorentz contraction of the containing box along the motion raises the count per volume by gamma.
key_equations.symbols: v speed of the dust in the observing frame

key_equations.name: Flux across constant-x surface (dust moving along x)
key_equations.meaning: Particles within v dt of the surface cross it in time dt; multiply by the moving-frame density.

key_equations.name: Flux for general velocity
key_equations.meaning: Only the component of velocity normal to the surface carries particles across it.
key_equations.symbols: v^x-bar x-component of the dust velocity; v its magnitude

key_equations.name: Number-flux vector
key_equations.meaning: Defines the four-vector that unifies density and flux.

key_equations.name: Four-velocity components
key_equations.meaning: Standard components of U in a frame where the particles have three-velocity v.

key_equations.name: Components of N
key_equations.meaning: Time component is the density, spatial components the fluxes, in any frame.

key_equations.name: Rest density from N
key_equations.meaning: The invariant length of N is the rest density, exactly as the length of four-momentum is rest mass.

key_equations.name: Unit normal one-form
key_equations.meaning: Normalizes the gradient of phi to represent the non-null surface phi = const uniquely (up to sign).
key_equations.symbols: phi function whose level set is the surface

key_equations.name: Magnitude of a one-form
key_equations.meaning: Norm of a one-form uses the inverse metric; absolute value covers timelike and spacelike normals.

key_equations.name: Hypersurface volume element
key_equations.meaning: Directed three-volume element in a hypersurface spanned by three distinct coordinates; the dx here are integration measures, not one-forms.

key_equations.name: Flux as contraction
key_equations.latex: \text{flux across }\phi=\text{const} = \langle\tilde n,\vec N\rangle,\qquad \langle\tilde{\mathrm d}\bar x,\vec N\rangle = N^{\alpha}(\tilde{\mathrm d}\bar x)_\alpha = N^{\bar x}
key_equations.meaning: The four-dimensional analogue of E.n: contract the matter's vector with the surface's normal one-form.

key_equations.name: Frame one-form
key_equations.latex: U_\alpha = \eta_{\alpha\beta}U^\beta,\quad U_0=-1,\ U_i=0 \;\Rightarrow\; \mathbf g(\vec U,\cdot) = -\tilde{\mathrm d}t
key_equations.meaning: The lowered four-velocity of an inertial observer is minus the gradient of its time coordinate.

key_equations.name: Energy via dt
key_equations.latex: E = \langle\tilde{\mathrm d}t,\vec p\rangle = p^0\quad(\text{cf. } E=-\vec p\cdot\vec U,\ \text{Eq. 2.35})
key_equations.meaning: Energy measured by a frame is the frame's time one-form acting on the four-momentum, with no minus sign.

key_equations.name: Energy density
key_equations.meaning: Defines the scalar rho.

key_equations.name: Dust energy density
key_equations.meaning: With no random motion, all energy is rest mass.

key_equations.name: Energy density in a moving frame
key_equations.latex: \frac{\rho}{1-v^2} = \text{energy density where the particles move with speed } v
key_equations.meaning: Two gamma factors (energy per particle and volume contraction) signal a second-rank tensor component.

key_equations.name: Definition of the stress-energy tensor
key_equations.latex: \mathbf T(\tilde{\mathrm d}x^\alpha,\tilde{\mathrm d}x^\beta) = T^{\alpha\beta} := \text{flux of }\alpha\text{-momentum across a surface of constant } x^\beta
key_equations.meaning: The component definition of T in any inertial frame; alpha-momentum means p^alpha = <dx^alpha, p>.

key_equations.name: Block meanings of T
key_equations.latex: T^{00}=\text{energy density},\quad T^{0i}=\text{energy flux across } x^i=\text{const},\quad T^{i0}=i\text{-momentum density},\quad T^{ij}=\text{flux of } i\text{-momentum across } x^j=\text{const}
key_equations.meaning: Dictionary of the four blocks of T.

key_equations.name: Dust in its MCRF
key_equations.meaning: No motion means no momentum and no flux.

key_equations.name: Dust stress-energy tensor
key_equations.latex: \mathbf T = \vec p\otimes\vec N = mn\,\vec U\otimes\vec U = \rho\,\vec U\otimes\vec U
key_equations.meaning: Covariant form matching the MCRF components.

key_equations.name: Dust components
key_equations.latex: T^{\alpha\beta} = \mathbf T(\tilde\omega^\alpha,\tilde\omega^\beta) = \rho\,\vec U(\tilde\omega^\alpha)\vec U(\tilde\omega^\beta) = \rho U^\alpha U^\beta
key_equations.meaning: Components in any frame follow by feeding basis one-forms.

key_equations.name: Dust components in a moving frame
key_equations.latex: T^{\bar0\bar0}=\frac{\rho}{1-v^2},\quad T^{\bar0\bar i}=\frac{\rho v^i}{1-v^2},\quad T^{\bar i\bar0}=\frac{\rho v^i}{1-v^2},\quad T^{\bar i\bar j}=\frac{\rho v^iv^j}{1-v^2}
key_equations.meaning: Energy density, energy flux, momentum density and momentum flux of moving dust, all carrying 1/(1-v^2) and manifestly symmetric. Shown corrected: the printed T^{i0} entry reads rho v^i (1-v^2), a typo confirmed on the page render.

key_equations.name: Table 4.1 relations
key_equations.meaning: Relations among MCRF fluid scalars: total energy density splits into rest-mass and internal parts.
key_equations.symbols: Pi internal energy per particle; rho_0 rest-mass density

key_equations.name: First law
key_equations.latex: \Delta E = \Delta Q - p\,\Delta V\quad\text{or}\quad \Delta Q = \Delta E + p\,\Delta V
key_equations.meaning: Energy balance of a fluid element in its MCRF: heat in, work out.
key_equations.symbols: Q heat absorbed; V element volume; E element energy

key_equations.name: Volume from particle number
key_equations.meaning: For a fixed number of particles N, volume changes are density changes.
key_equations.symbols: N number of particles in the element (not the vector)

key_equations.name: Heat in terms of rho and n
key_equations.latex: E=\rho V=\rho N/n,\quad \Delta E=\rho\Delta V+V\Delta\rho\ \Rightarrow\ \Delta Q=\frac{N}{n}\Delta\rho - N(\rho+p)\frac{\Delta n}{n^2}
key_equations.meaning: Intermediate step eliminating E and V.

key_equations.name: First law per particle
key_equations.meaning: Heat per particle q = Q/N expressed through changes of rho and n.

key_equations.name: Temperature and entropy via integrating factor
key_equations.meaning: The first-law form has an integrating factor that defines temperature T and specific entropy S.
key_equations.symbols: T temperature; S entropy per particle

key_equations.name: Heat and entropy
key_equations.meaning: Heat absorbed per particle is temperature times increase in specific entropy.

key_equations.name: Stress as force per area
key_equations.latex: T^{ij} = F^i/A\quad(\text{across a surface of constant } x^j)
key_equations.meaning: Force between adjacent elements is a momentum flux.
key_equations.symbols: F force of element A on neighbour B; A interface area

key_equations.name: Torque on a small cube
key_equations.meaning: Net torque about the z axis from the four side faces of a cube of side l.

key_equations.name: Moment of inertia (as printed)
key_equations.meaning: Book states I is proportional to mass times l^2; since the mass is rho l^3, the correct scaling is I proportional to rho l^5, which is what makes Eq. 4.28 come out as written.

key_equations.name: Angular acceleration of the element
key_equations.meaning: Diverges as l -> 0 unless the stresses are symmetric.

key_equations.name: Symmetry of stresses
key_equations.meaning: Holds for any material, relativistic or Newtonian.

key_equations.name: Energy flux equals momentum density
key_equations.meaning: Moving energy is moving mass, so energy flux and momentum density coincide.

key_equations.name: Energy balance of a cubical element
key_equations.meaning: Rate of change of energy inside equals net inflow through the faces.

key_equations.name: Differential energy balance

key_equations.name: Energy conservation
key_equations.meaning: Local conservation of energy as a four-divergence.

key_equations.name: Energy-momentum conservation
key_equations.meaning: Local conservation of all four components of four-momentum for any isolated material in SR.

key_equations.name: Particle conservation
key_equations.meaning: Particles (baryons) are neither created nor destroyed.

key_equations.name: Perfect fluid in the MCRF
key_equations.meaning: No heat flux, isotropic stress.

key_equations.meaning: Component expression that reproduces Eq. 4.36 in the MCRF and holds in any frame.

key_equations.name: Adiabatic flow
key_equations.meaning: A particle-conserving perfect fluid conserves specific entropy along each world line.

key_equations.meaning: Momentum components of Eq. 4.45.

key_equations.meaning: Derivative of (rho+p)/n multiplies U^i = 0 and drops; derivatives of U^i survive.

key_equations.meaning: Lowering a spatial index changes nothing in Minkowski components.

key_equations.meaning: Pressure gradients accelerate a perfect-fluid element whose inertia per unit volume is rho + p.

key_equations.meaning: Nonrelativistic limit (no external forces).
key_equations.symbols: a fluid acceleration; rho mass density

key_equations.name: Advective acceleration (corrected)
key_equations.meaning: Acceleration following the fluid. The book prints (a.grad)a; the correct expression, used in Exercise 4.17, has v in both places.

key_equations.name: Pressure gradient needed for support
key_equations.meaning: Given the acceleration gravity would produce, the required pressure gradient is larger than Newtonian because rho+p > rho.

key_equations.name: Gauss' law in spacetime
key_equations.meaning: Four-volume integral of a divergence equals the outward flux through the bounding hypersurface.
key_equations.symbols: n_alpha outward unit normal one-form; d^3S three-volume element of the boundary

key_equations.latex: \int\left[V^0(t_2)-V^0(t_1)\right]\mathrm dx\,\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dz + \int\left[V^x(x_2)-V^x(x_1)\right]\mathrm dt\,\mathrm dy\,\mathrm dz + \dots

key_equations.name: Observer-measured density (Exercise 4.4)
key_equations.meaning: Density seen by an arbitrary observer is minus the projection of N on that observer's four-velocity.

key_equations.name: First law as one-forms (Exercise 4.8)

key_equations.meaning: The thermodynamic relation holds as an equation between one-forms; the heat one-form is not a gradient.

key_equations.name: Newtonian continuity equation (Exercise 4.10)
key_equations.meaning: Slow-motion limit of Eq. 4.35.

key_equations.name: Advective derivative (Exercise 4.17)
key_equations.meaning: Low-velocity limit of the four-acceleration U^mu_{,beta}U^beta.
