figures.label: Figure 4.1 (left panel)
figures.caption_paraphrase: The same set of particles is counted in a box in the rest frame; how many per unit volume depends on which frame measures the box.
figures.visual_description: Three-dimensional axes: x toward the viewer at lower left, y to the right, z up. A cube floats above the axes with edges labelled Delta y (front bottom), Delta z (right vertical) and Delta x (receding depth edge); 'In MCRF' is printed under it. Above the panel, printed as part of the figure, is the note that the box holds N particles, so n = N/(Delta x Delta y Delta z).
figures.what_it_teaches: Rest-frame number density is a simple count divided by a rest-frame volume.

redesign.idea: Live boost of a particle-filled box: a 3D cloud of dots in a cube; a velocity slider squashes the cube along the motion while the dots stay the same set, and a readout shows count, volume and density with the factor gamma highlighted.
redesign.interaction: Drag v from 0 to 0.99; toggle between rest-frame and lab-frame views; click to count particles; a second readout shows energy per particle so the learner sees gamma twice for energy density.

figures.label: Figure 4.1 (right panel)
figures.caption_paraphrase: In the frame where the particles move, the box holding the same particles is Lorentz contracted, so the density is higher.
figures.visual_description: Same axes with barred labels x-bar, y-bar, z-bar and 'in O-bar' beneath. The box is drawn as a tall, narrow slab (edges Delta x-bar, Delta y-bar, Delta z-bar) instead of a cube, so it visibly holds the same particles in a smaller volume; the sketch does not mark which axis the motion is along, so the squashing is schematic. Printed above: the box contains the same particles, now n = N/(Delta x-bar Delta y-bar Delta z-bar).
figures.what_it_teaches: Density is frame dependent through Lorentz contraction; only the rest-frame value n is a scalar.

redesign.idea: Merge with the left panel into one animation (see left-panel redesign) so the contraction is seen continuously rather than as two static states.
redesign.interaction: Same controls as the left panel; add a 'show both frames side by side' toggle.

figures.label: Figure 4.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: When all particles move along x, the ones that reach a surface within a time interval are exactly those lying within v times that interval of it.
figures.visual_description: Axes x-bar (horizontal) and y-bar (vertical). A long vertical line at the right labelled S is the surface perpendicular to x-bar. Four dots each carry a short rightward arrow: one at lower left, one just below the x-bar axis, and two inside a dashed rectangle that sits against S. A bracket over the rectangle gives its length as v Delta t-bar, and a label beside S reads Delta A = Delta y Delta z.
figures.what_it_teaches: Flux = density x normal speed, derived by picturing the volume swept toward the surface.

redesign.idea: Particle stream through a gate: 2D dots drift toward a surface; a highlighted 'capture box' of length v dt shows which dots will cross in the next dt, and a counter accumulates crossings per unit time and area.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for v, dt and density; press play to watch the boxed dots cross while the running flux converges to n gamma v; rotate the surface to see flux drop as the normal component of velocity falls.

figures.label: Figure 4.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: With a velocity that has components both along and parallel to the surface, only the component normal to the surface determines how many particles cross.
figures.visual_description: Axes x-bar and y-bar with a vertical surface line on the right, an arrow labelled A pointing to it from below. Several parallel arrows slant up and to the right (velocity with x and y components). A dashed parallelogram with slanted sides rests against the surface; beneath it, facing arrows mark its horizontal width as v^x-bar Delta t-bar; a label beside the surface reads Delta A = Delta y-bar Delta z-bar.
figures.what_it_teaches: The crossing region is a parallelepiped whose height, not slant length, sets the count, so flux^x = n gamma v^x.

redesign.idea: Extend the Figure 4.2 widget with a draggable velocity arrow: the capture region shears into a parallelogram and its base-times-height area updates, making plain that only v^x matters.
redesign.interaction: Drag the velocity arrow tip; toggle 'show slant length vs. height'; readout compares flux with n gamma v and n gamma v^x.

figures.label: Figure 4.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: The flux construction of Figure 4.2 redrawn in a spacetime diagram with y suppressed.
figures.visual_description: Spacetime axes t-bar (vertical) and x-bar (horizontal). A vertical line S at fixed x-bar is the world line of the surface. A bundle of five parallel slanted straight lines, starting from a bracket labelled 'Particles' on the x-bar axis, runs up and to the right and crosses S. Two horizontal dashed lines mark an interval Delta t-bar, bracketed on the t-bar axis; the particle world lines cross S between the dashed lines.
figures.what_it_teaches: Spatial flux is the number of world lines piercing a unit piece (dt dy dz) of the surface's world-tube.

redesign.idea: Rotatable 3D spacetime (t, x, y) showing a sheet x = const and a sheet t = const with a bundle of particle world lines; a unit patch on either sheet counts piercings, and the learner can tilt world lines by changing velocity.
redesign.interaction: Toggle which hypersurface is active (x = const or t = const); drag a velocity slider; move the unit patch; readouts show N^x and N^0 and their match with <n~, N>.

figures.label: Figure 4.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: Number density viewed as the flux of world lines across a surface of constant time.
figures.visual_description: Axes t-bar and x-bar. A horizontal line labelled S at a fixed t-bar represents a surface of simultaneity. The same bundle of five slanted particle world lines, starting from a bracket 'Particles' near the x-bar axis, crosses S. Two vertical dashed lines drop from the outermost crossing points to the x-bar axis, marking an interval Delta x-bar.
figures.what_it_teaches: Counting world lines through a unit spatial volume at one time is the density: the time component of the flux vector.

redesign.idea: Covered by the 3D hypersurface widget proposed for Figure 4.4; add a 2D mode that smoothly rotates the counting line from vertical (flux) to horizontal (density).
redesign.interaction: Angle slider rotates the counting surface through timelike, null and spacelike orientations, showing the unit-normal normalization failing at the null angle.

figures.label: Figure 4.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Neighbouring fluid element A pushes on B across their shared face with a force whose direction depends on the medium and on other forces.
figures.visual_description: xyz axes at left. Two cubes A and B joined into one long box, their shared face S drawn with dashed hidden edges. A bold arrow F starts on the shared face and points into B, tilted slightly off the face normal.
figures.what_it_teaches: Stress T^{ij} is momentum per unit time per unit area transferred across an interface, and it need not be normal to the interface.

redesign.idea: Stress explorer: two adjacent blocks with a draggable force arrow on the interface; the arrow splits into normal (pressure-like) and tangential (shear) parts, and a 3x3 stress matrix highlights which entry each part fills.
redesign.interaction: Drag the force direction and magnitude; rotate the interface orientation (x, y or z face); toggle 'fluid' to force the tangential part to zero and watch the matrix go diagonal.

figures.label: Figure 4.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: A small cubical fluid element used for the torque argument.
figures.visual_description: xyz axes at lower left. A cube with all edges labelled l. Circled numbers mark faces: 1 on the front face (facing +x) and 2 on the right face (facing +y); arrows with circled 3 and 4 point to the hidden back face (facing -x) and the left face (facing -y).
figures.what_it_teaches: Labels the faces whose forces produce torques about z; used to show asymmetric stresses would spin tiny elements infinitely fast.

redesign.idea: Shrinking-cube spin test: a cube with adjustable T^{xy} and T^{yx}; face forces drawn as arrows; as the learner shrinks l, a plot of angular acceleration (proportional to 1/l^2) blows up unless the two stresses are set equal.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for T^{xy}, T^{yx} and l (log scale); animated spin rate; a 'snap symmetric' button zeroes the torque.

figures.label: Figure 4.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: Cross-section at constant z of a cubical fluid element, used for energy bookkeeping.
figures.visual_description: x and y axes with a square from 0 to l along each. Its sides are numbered 1 (bottom, y = 0), 2 (right, x = l), 3 (top, y = l) and 4 (left, x = 0).
figures.what_it_teaches: Energy entering through face 4 and leaving through face 2 (and likewise in y) changes the energy inside; the limit gives the divergence law.

redesign.idea: Flux ledger: a 2D grid cell over a heat-map of energy density with arrows of T^{0i} on its edges; inflow and outflow bars update and the interior shading changes at their net rate; shrinking the cell turns the difference quotient into the divergence.
redesign.interaction: Draw or choose a flux field; drag and resize the cell; play time evolution; a side panel shows the discrete sum vs. -div T^{0i} converging.

figures.label: Figure 4.9
figures.caption_paraphrase: A region of spacetime and the three-surface that bounds it.
figures.visual_description: Axes t (vertical) and x (horizontal). A hatched rectangle labelled 'four-volume' spans x_1 to x_2 horizontally and t_1 to t_2 vertically. A label 'three-surface' has curved arrows pointing to the top edge and the left edge of the rectangle.
figures.what_it_teaches: Gauss' law in spacetime: the boundary consists of constant-time faces (contents at two times) and constant-x faces (walls through which flux passes), each with an outward normal.
concepts: outward normal orientation on spacetime boundaries

redesign.idea: Spacetime box accountant: particle world lines pass through a draggable rectangle in (t, x); every crossing of the boundary is tagged +1 or -1 according to the outward normal (+-dt, +-dx), and the total is shown to be zero while the count at t_2 minus the count at t_1 equals net wall inflow.
redesign.interaction: Drag the corners of the box; add sources (Exercise 4.20) to break conservation; toggle display of normal one-forms as arrows/stacks on each face.

figures.label: Table 4.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: Macroscopic MCRF quantities used to describe a single-component fluid.
figures.visual_description: A shaded three-column table (Symbol, Name, Definition) with nine rows: four-velocity U of the element, number density n, flux vector N = nU, energy density rho (all forms of mass-energy), internal energy per particle Pi = rho/n - m, rest-mass density rho_0 = mn with rho = rho_0 + n Pi, temperature T, pressure p, specific entropy S. Exported as schutz/pages/page-112/tbl-4.html.
figures.what_it_teaches: Collects the convention that every fluid scalar is an MCRF value and fixes the relations among rho, rho_0, Pi and n.

redesign.idea: Energy-budget bar for one fluid element: stacked bar of rest-mass energy and internal energy per unit volume, updating as the learner heats or compresses the element, with the table's symbols attached to each segment.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for n and temperature (or Pi); hover a segment to see its definition and symbol.

worked_examples.label: Density of moving dust (Eq. 4.2)
worked_examples.problem: Find the number of dust particles per unit volume in a frame where they all move with speed v.
worked_examples.method: Take a rest-frame box of volume dx dy dz holding the particles; in the moving frame the dimension along the motion contracts by sqrt(1-v^2) while transverse ones do not; the particle count is unchanged.
worked_examples.key_insight: Counting is invariant, volume is not, so density acquires exactly one gamma factor.

worked_examples.label: Flux of dust across a surface (Eq. 4.3)
worked_examples.problem: Compute the particle flux across a surface of constant x in a frame where dust moves with velocity v.
worked_examples.method: Particles that cross area dA in time dt are those in a prism adjacent to the surface; for motion along x its volume is v dt dA, for general motion it is a parallelepiped of height v^x dt. Multiply by the moving-frame density and divide by dt dA.
worked_examples.key_insight: Only the normal velocity component matters, and density brings its own gamma.

worked_examples.label: Components and norm of N (Eqs. 4.5-4.6)
worked_examples.problem: Show that density and fluxes form a four-vector and extract the rest density invariantly.
worked_examples.method: Multiply the known components of U in the moving frame by n; compare term by term with Eqs. 4.2-4.3; compute N.N = n^2 U.U = -n^2.
worked_examples.key_insight: The Galilean split between an invariant density and a frame-dependent flux dissolves into components of one vector.
worked_examples.result: N -> (n gamma, n gamma v^i); n = (-N.N)^{1/2}

worked_examples.label: Flux via a normal one-form
worked_examples.problem: Verify that contracting N with a surface's unit normal one-form gives the flux across that surface.
worked_examples.method: Take phi = x: dx has components (0,1,0,0) and unit norm, so <dx, N> = N^x, the flux already found. Take phi = t: <dt, N> = N^0, the density.
worked_examples.key_insight: The same contraction handles spatial fluxes and density; the surface and the matter are separate objects.
concepts: flux as contraction of one-form with vector

worked_examples.label: Energy density of moving dust (Eq. 4.13)
worked_examples.problem: Find the energy per unit volume of dust in a frame where it moves with speed v.
worked_examples.method: Density is n gamma; energy per particle is m gamma; multiply.
worked_examples.key_insight: Two gamma factors mean energy density cannot be a four-vector component; it must come from a second-rank tensor.

worked_examples.label: Stress-energy tensor of dust (Eqs. 4.19-4.21)
worked_examples.problem: Construct T for dust and give its components in any frame.
worked_examples.method: In the MCRF only T^{00} = mn is non-zero. The outer product p(x)N = mn U(x)U has exactly these MCRF components, so the tensors agree; evaluating on basis one-forms gives rho U^aU^b, and inserting boosted U gives each block. Exercise 4.21(a)-(c) extends this to beams and rotating rings.
worked_examples.key_insight: Match components in one convenient frame, then the tensor equation holds everywhere.
worked_examples.result: T^{00} = rho gamma^2, T^{0i} = T^{i0} = rho gamma^2 v^i, T^{ij} = rho gamma^2 v^iv^j

worked_examples.label: First law in fluid variables (Eqs. 4.22-4.26)
worked_examples.problem: Express the heat absorbed by a fluid element with fixed particle number in terms of changes in rho and n, and introduce T and S.
worked_examples.method: Start from dQ = dE + p dV; substitute V = N/n, dV = -N dn/n^2, E = rho N/n; divide by N to get n dq = drho - (rho+p)dn/n; note the right side is a form in two variables, so it equals A dB; name A/n temperature and B specific entropy.
worked_examples.key_insight: Thermodynamic temperature and entropy can be introduced purely as bookkeeping devices of energy conservation.
worked_examples.result: drho - (rho+p) dn/n = nT dS; dq = T dS
concepts: first law of thermodynamics for a fluid element
temperature and specific entropy via integrating factor

worked_examples.label: Symmetry of stresses from torques (Eqs. 4.27-4.29)
worked_examples.problem: Prove that T^{ij} = T^{ji} for any material.
worked_examples.method: Put the origin at the centre of a cube of side l. Forces on opposite faces nearly cancel (else infinite linear acceleration). Face forces act at face centres l/2 from the axis: faces normal to x contribute -(1/2)l^3 T^{yx} each, faces normal to y contribute +(1/2)l^3 T^{xy} each, so tau_z = l^3(T^{xy} - T^{yx}). Moment of inertia scales as mass times l^2, i.e. as l^5, so angular acceleration scales as (T^{xy} - T^{yx})/l^2 and diverges as l -> 0 unless the stresses are equal.
worked_examples.key_insight: Torque scales as l^3 but inertia as l^5; only symmetric stress avoids ever-faster spinning of ever-smaller elements.

worked_examples.label: Energy conservation from a box (Eqs. 4.30-4.34)
worked_examples.problem: Derive a local conservation law for energy and momentum.
worked_examples.method: Sum energy inflow minus outflow through the six faces of a cube (each face flux times l^2); equate to d(l^3 T^{00})/dt; divide by l^3 and let l -> 0 to turn differences into partial derivatives; repeat with a momentum index.
worked_examples.key_insight: A conservation law in differential form is a four-divergence: rate of change of density plus divergence of flux vanishes.

worked_examples.label: Perfect-fluid tensor from physical conditions (Eqs. 4.36-4.38)
worked_examples.problem: Find the stress-energy tensor of a fluid with no viscosity and no heat conduction.
worked_examples.method: No heat conduction sets T^{0i} = 0 in the MCRF. No viscosity makes T^{ij} diagonal for every orientation of axes; only multiples of delta^{ij} have this property (Exercise 4.11), so T^{ij} = p delta^{ij}. Guess (rho+p)U^aU^b + p eta^{ab} and check entries in the MCRF, e.g. 00: (rho+p)(1) + p(-1) = rho; ij: 0 + p delta^{ij}.
worked_examples.key_insight: Physical restrictions reduce ten functions to rho, p and U; the invariant form follows by matching in the MCRF.

worked_examples.label: Adiabatic flow from energy conservation (Eqs. 4.39-4.50)
worked_examples.problem: Extract the component of T^{ab}_{,b} = 0 along the flow for a perfect fluid and interpret it.
worked_examples.method: Use (nU^b)_{,b} = 0 to write the inertial term as nU^b((rho+p)U^a/n)_{,b}; prove U^a_{,b}U_a = 0 by differentiating U.U = -1; contract with U_a so that derivatives of U drop and U.U = -1 remains; the pressure term becomes dp/dtau; simplify to drho/dtau = ((rho+p)/n) dn/dtau and compare with nT dS.
worked_examples.key_insight: Energy conservation along the flow is the first law, and for a perfect fluid it says specific entropy is carried unchanged.
concepts: orthogonality of four-velocity and its gradient

worked_examples.label: Relativistic Euler equation (Eqs. 4.51-4.54)
worked_examples.problem: Extract the momentum components of the perfect-fluid conservation law.
worked_examples.method: Work in the MCRF at the event: U^i = 0 but U^i_{,b} need not vanish. The derivative of (rho+p)/n multiplies U^i and drops; what remains is (rho+p)U^i_{,b}U^b + p_{,b}eta^{ib} = 0; lower i and recognize U_{i,b}U^b as the four-acceleration.
worked_examples.key_insight: Pressure contributes to inertia: rho + p replaces rho in F = ma.

worked_examples.label: Pressure gradient needed to support a star (§4.8)
worked_examples.problem: Estimate how the pressure gradient required to hold up a dense star differs from the Newtonian case.
worked_examples.method: Let a_i be the acceleration an element would have under gravity alone; support requires a pressure gradient producing -a_i, so p_{,i} = -(rho+p)a_i. Compare with Newtonian p_{,i} = -rho a_i and add the fact that pressure itself gravitates.
worked_examples.key_insight: Both the inertial and the gravitational roles of pressure push the requirement up, so when p approaches rho support fails.
concepts: pressure as a source of gravity

worked_examples.label: Gauss' law on a coordinate box (Eq. 4.58)
worked_examples.problem: Evaluate the boundary integral of the four-dimensional divergence theorem for a box bounded by t_1, t_2, x_1, x_2 (and y, z faces).
worked_examples.method: Assign outward normals: dt at t_2, -dt at t_1, dx at x_2, -dx at x_1; contract with V to get +-V^0 and +-V^x; group into differences across the box.
worked_examples.key_insight: For a conserved current, the change of the amount inside between two times equals the net flux through the spatial walls.
worked_examples.result: Integral of [V^0(t_2) - V^0(t_1)] dx dy dz + integral of [V^x(x_2) - V^x(x_1)] dt dy dz + ... = 0 when V^a_{,a} = 0
concepts: outward normal orientation on spacetime boundaries

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The electric flux E.n through a surface in Gauss' law
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: flux as contraction of one-form with vector
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: The particle flux across a hypersurface is presented as the exact spacetime counterpart: contract the matter's four-vector with the surface's unit normal one-form.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: In spacetime the normal is naturally a one-form, not a vector, and for null surfaces no unit normal exists; sign and orientation subtleties of Lorentzian normals have no 3D analogue.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Split-screen: 3D E-field through a tilted patch beside a spacetime world-line bundle through a tilted hypersurface, with the same 'dot with the normal' readout in both.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Rest density n versus measured density is like rest mass versus energy
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Shows why n is a scalar even though every observer measures a different density: it is the invariant length of N, as rest mass is the length of p.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Mass has no analogue of 'flux across a surface'; the analogy covers invariance, not the geometry of surfaces.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Unifying density and flux into N parallels unifying energy and momentum into the four-momentum
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Frames the new vector as another instance of relativity merging quantities that were separate in Galilean physics.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Energy and momentum were both frame dependent before relativity, whereas Galilean density was invariant; the unification here also changes the invariance status of density.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A lake's gravity depends on bulk properties, not on where each water molecule is
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Motivates describing matter by averaged fields when computing its gravitational field.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Says nothing about the conditions under which averaging fails (rarefied gases, Exercise 4.1 cases).

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Rigidity as the ability of neighbouring blocks to stop each other sliding
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Reduces the solid/fluid distinction to the presence of tangential forces at interfaces, which later become the off-diagonal stresses.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Real fluids have viscosity and solids creep; the classification is a matter of degree and timescale.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Two stacked blocks with an adjustable friction-like shear coupling; push the top block and watch it slide (fluid) or drag the lower block (solid).

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The one-form dt as a stack of surfaces of simultaneity that defines a frame
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Gives a picture in which an observer's frame is literally its family of 'now' slices, making E = <dt, p> a count of how many slices p pierces.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Fixes the frame only up to spatial rotations, and in curved spacetime a global time function may not exist.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Stack of tilted simultaneity sheets for a chosen boost; drag a four-momentum arrow and count the sheets it crosses to read off E.

analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Grounds the spatial block of T in a quantity a materials engineer already uses; the relativistic tensor inherits its name.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Relativistic T also includes energy and momentum densities and requires T^{0i} = T^{i0}, which has no Newtonian counterpart.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: F = ma for a fluid element, with a pressure difference as the net force
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Reads (rho+p)a_i = -p_{,i} as Newton's law: an element pushed equally from both sides feels no force, so only the gradient of p accelerates it, and rho + p is the mass per volume.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: The 'mass' rho+p is not a rest mass of anything; it includes pressure, and in GR pressure also gravitates.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Row of fluid parcels with pressure arrows on both faces; adjust a pressure profile and see the net force and resulting acceleration, with a toggle to add p to the inertia.

analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: equality of energy flux and momentum density
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Justifies T^{0i} = T^{i0} in one step: energy flux = energy density x speed = mass density x speed = momentum density.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Heuristic; it relies on c = 1 and on identifying a single transport speed, and does not by itself handle stress contributions.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The number of particles per unit volume is the same for all observers.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Measured density is larger by gamma in a frame where the particles move, because the volume Lorentz contracts; only the MCRF value n is invariant.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In Galilean physics density is an invariant scalar and counting feels observer independent.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: 'Frame independent' means a quantity has the same components in all frames.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A vector or tensor is frame independent as a geometric object; its components change with the frame. Invariance of components is special to scalars.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Everyday language equates 'independent of frame' with 'same numbers'.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Flux across a surface of constant x is 'flux in the x direction', so it is naturally a vector along x.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: A flux is defined relative to a surface, which is represented by a normal one-form; the flux is the contraction of N with that one-form (Exercise 4.2).
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In Euclidean 3D with an orthonormal basis, normals and directions are interchangeable.
concepts: flux as contraction of one-form with vector

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Energy density is the time component of some four-vector, like number density.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Energy density of moving dust carries two gamma factors, so it is the 00 component of a second-rank tensor, not a vector component.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Energy is the time component of four-momentum and density is the time component of N, so their combination seems vector-like.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A single MCRF can be used for the whole fluid at all times.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The MCRF belongs to one element at one moment; different elements move relative to each other and accelerate, so each has its own, changing MCRF.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: For a single particle in uniform motion one rest frame suffices forever.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Because U^i = 0 in the MCRF, the derivatives U^i_{,b} also vanish there.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: U^i vanishes only at the chosen event in that frame; neighbouring events have different velocities, so its gradient (and the acceleration) can be non-zero.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Setting a quantity to zero in a convenient frame feels like setting it zero identically.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Pressure requires collisions or forces between particles; a collisionless gas has no pressure.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Pressure is momentum flux in the MCRF; particles carrying momentum across a surface produce it just as forces do. Only matter with no random motion (dust) is pressureless.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: School pictures of pressure emphasize molecules hitting walls or each other.
concepts: pressure as momentum flux from random motion

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Stress symmetry is a special property of fluids.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The torque argument uses no material properties, so T^{ij} = T^{ji} holds for solids as well, in Newtonian physics and relativity.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The proof appears in a chapter about fluids.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The force on a fluid element is -p, the pressure itself.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Pressure from the neighbour on one side is balanced by the neighbour on the other; only the change of p across the element gives a net force, -grad p.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Pressure is described as a force per area, so it is natural to treat it as the force.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Gravity in a relativistic theory is sourced by mass density (or by energy density T^{00}).
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Rest mass is not separately conserved in relativity and a rest-mass source conflicts with experiment; T^{00} alone is frame dependent. The source must be the whole tensor T, so momenta, stresses and pressure gravitate.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Newtonian gravity uses mass density, and E = mc^2 suggests just swapping in energy density.
concepts: stress-energy tensor as source of gravity
pressure as a source of gravity

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: More pressure always makes a star more stable against collapse.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: In GR pressure adds both inertia and gravitational pull; when p is comparable with rho, increasing the pressure increases the gravity it must fight and no equilibrium exists.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In Newtonian stars pressure is purely supportive.
concepts: pressure as a source of gravity

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The unit normal one-form n~ and the number density n are related.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They are unrelated; the shared letter is a historical accident.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The outward normal on every face of a spacetime box points toward the future or toward larger coordinates.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Outward means away from the enclosed region: on the earlier constant-time face the outward normal one-form is -dt (toward the past), on the smaller-x wall it is -dx.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Time is usually pictured as flowing only forward, so a past-directed normal seems wrong.
concepts: outward normal orientation on spacetime boundaries

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: T^{ab}_{,b} = 0 means the energy density at each point is constant in time.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: It says the local rate of change of energy density is exactly compensated by the divergence of energy flux; energy can move around but not appear or disappear.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The word 'conservation' is often heard as 'staying put'.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Every surface has a unit normal one-form.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: For a null hypersurface the gradient has zero norm and cannot be normalized; the book restricts Eq. 4.7 to non-null surfaces.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In Euclidean geometry every non-degenerate surface has a unit normal.

misconceptions_addressed.correction: Dust has no random (thermal) motion relative to its local rest frame; its bulk flow can be arbitrarily fast.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The everyday meaning of dust evokes something at rest.

thought_experiments.name: Whirling fluid elements
thought_experiments.setup: Imagine the stresses on a small cube were not symmetric and shrink the cube: torque falls as l^3 but moment of inertia as l^5.
thought_experiments.lesson: Ever smaller elements would spin ever faster, which is absurd, so stresses are symmetric in any material.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Fractal-zoom animation into a fluid showing nested cubes spinning faster at each zoom level when asymmetry is switched on, and all still when it is off.

thought_experiments.name: Unbalanced forces on a vanishing element
thought_experiments.setup: Suppose forces on opposite faces of a small element did not nearly cancel as its size goes to zero.
thought_experiments.lesson: A finite net force on a vanishing mass would produce infinite acceleration, so opposite face forces cancel to leading order.

thought_experiments.name: Counting world lines through a hypersurface
thought_experiments.setup: Draw the world lines of dust and a surface; count how many world lines pierce a unit piece of the surface's world-tube, then of a constant-time slice.
thought_experiments.lesson: Flux and density are the same kind of quantity: world-line crossings of a hypersurface.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Covered by the hypersurface-counting widget in the Figure 4.4 redesign.

thought_experiments.name: Alternative sources for relativistic gravity
thought_experiments.setup: Try to build a relativistic gravity theory sourced by rest-mass density, or by energy density T^{00} alone.
thought_experiments.lesson: The first ignores interconvertibility of mass and energy and fails precision tests; the second needs a preferred frame; only the whole T works.
concepts: stress-energy tensor as source of gravity

thought_experiments.name: Holding up an ever-denser star
thought_experiments.setup: Increase the central density of a star and ask what pressure gradient keeps each element from falling, remembering that pressure gravitates and adds inertia.
thought_experiments.lesson: The needed pressure feeds back into gravity; once p nears rho the feedback runs away and collapse is unavoidable.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Feedback-loop toy: slider for compactness; iterative bars show pressure needed and the extra gravity it generates, converging for low compactness and diverging beyond a threshold.

historical_notes.event: Einstein guessed that the source of gravity in a relativistic theory must be the entire stress-energy tensor, and combined this with curved-space geometry to reach GR.
historical_notes.significance: Explains why the chapter's careful construction of T is a prerequisite for the field equations.

historical_notes.event: Before relativity, particle flux was treated as a three-vector defined relative to a chosen inertial frame, separate from an invariant number density.
historical_notes.significance: Sets up the conceptual gain of the four-vector N.

historical_notes.event: Grand unified theories suggest the proton may decay and black-hole formation followed by evaporation would not conserve baryons, but no violation of baryon number had been observed.
historical_notes.significance: Justifies assuming N^a_{,a} = 0 for astrophysical fluids while flagging its theoretical limits.

applications_and_observations.topic: Stars and other astrophysical gravity sources modelled as perfect fluids
applications_and_observations.details: The chapter opens by noting that in many astrophysical GR problems a perfect fluid is a good first model of the source; §4.8 applies the relativistic Euler equation to hydrostatic support of dense stars.

applications_and_observations.topic: Neutron stars and relativistic gases, where p is comparable with rho
applications_and_observations.details: Pressure becomes a sizeable fraction of the energy density only in matter as dense as a neutron star's or so hot that its particles move near light speed; in those regimes relativistic pressure effects control stability. Note that even an ultra-relativistic gas reaches only p = rho/3, so 'p comparable with rho' means 'of the same order', not equal.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Own estimate for context (SI, p/(rho c^2)): water at 1 atm ~ 1e-15; centre of the Sun ~ 1e-6 to 1e-5; neutron-star core ~ 0.1-0.5; photon gas exactly 1/3.

applications_and_observations.topic: Baryon number conservation and proton decay searches
applications_and_observations.details: Particle number conservation is justified by baryon conservation; theoretical violations (grand unification, black-hole evaporation, Chapter 11) had not been observed.

applications_and_observations.topic: Collisionless systems: black-body radiation, rarefied plasmas, galaxies, globular clusters
applications_and_observations.details: Exercise 4.22 shows an isotropic velocity distribution gives a perfect-fluid tensor; for particles of one speed p and rho follow from m, v, n, and a photon gas has p = rho/3.

applications_and_observations.topic: Apparent brightness of a moving star
applications_and_observations.details: Exercise 4.24 builds the frame-invariant stress-energy tensor of starlight and asks how the measured energy flux T^{0x} depends on the observer's recession speed.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: Rest frame: T^{00} = T^{0x} = T^{xx} = L/(4 pi x^2)

applications_and_observations.topic: Tests of the continuum approximation on everyday systems
applications_and_observations.details: Exercise 4.1 has the reader judge planetary motion, lava flow, rush-hour and stop-sign traffic, and plasma dynamics against the element criterion.

notation_and_conventions.convention: c = 1 throughout; speeds are dimensionless and gamma is written (1-v^2)^{-1/2}, equal to the boost matrix entry Lambda^0-bar_0.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Compare with p and rho in SI by dividing p by rho c^2.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Minkowski metric eta = diag(-1, 1, 1, 1): U.U = -1, N.N = -n^2, lowered four-velocity components (-1, 0, 0, 0) in the rest frame, eta^{00} = -1 used in checking Eq. 4.37.
Vectors carry an arrow (N, U, p); one-forms a tilde (n~, dt, omega~^alpha); tensors are bold (T, g); g^{-1} is the inverse metric with components eta^{ab}; (2 0) tensors take two one-form arguments.
A comma denotes a partial derivative with respect to a coordinate: T^{ab}_{,b} = dT^{ab}/dx^b, phi_{,a} = d phi/dx^a.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Becomes a semicolon (covariant derivative) in curved spacetime later in the book.

notation_and_conventions.convention: First index labels the component of four-momentum, second labels the coordinate held constant on the surface crossed.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Harmless in practice because T is proven symmetric.

notation_and_conventions.convention: O-bar denotes the frame in which the dust moves, and barred indices label components in that frame; the printed book uses a bar throughout.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The reading-copy export often turns the bar into a tilde or a vector arrow (e.g. O~, x~); these are OCR artifacts, not a different frame or a one-form.

notation_and_conventions.convention: rho is MCRF energy density including rest mass, thermal and other energies; rho_0 = mn is rest-mass density and Pi internal energy per particle.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Differs from Newtonian usage where rho is mass density.

notation_and_conventions.convention: n: rest number density; n~: unit normal one-form. T: temperature (italic) and stress-energy tensor (bold). N: particle count in an element and the flux vector. S: specific entropy and a surface. A: an interface area and a fluid element label. rho: charge density in Exercise 4.25.
notation_and_conventions.notes: The book explicitly warns only about n versus n~.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Greek indices run over 0-3, Latin indices over spatial 1-3; summation convention applies.
d^4x is the coordinate four-volume; d^3S the three-volume of a bounding hypersurface; plain dx^a in Eq. 4.9 are integration infinitesimals, not basis one-forms.

margin_notes.summary: Admits the relativists' use of 'dust' for pressureless matter has an obscure origin unrelated to windowsill dust.
Warns that the unit normal one-form n~ and the number density n share a letter only by historical accident.
Clarifies that the dx's in the volume element are integration infinitesimals, not gradient one-forms.
Contrasts E = <dt, p> with the earlier E = -p.U (Eq. 2.35), noting the absence of the awkward minus sign.
Proof that the component definition of T really gives a tensor (linearity in both slots) is left to Exercise 4.5.
Asserts without proof that the T and S introduced via the integrating factor coincide with thermodynamic temperature and the second-law entropy, and that the second law will not be used.
Invites the reader to think through why forces normal to element faces give a diagonal stress matrix, a fact used for perfect fluids.
Explains baryons for readers new to particle physics and why baryon number conservation is safe despite theoretical exceptions such as black-hole evaporation (Chapter 11).
Aside on the meaning of pressure: dust is the pressureless perfect fluid; any random motion gives pressure, since pressure is momentum flux regardless of mechanism.
Mentions that a rest-mass-sourced gravity theory would violate very-high-precision experiments to be discussed later.

Bibliography: Fermi for thermodynamics, Landau & Lifshitz for fluids and fields, Jackson for electromagnetism, Israel & Stewart for dissipative relativistic fluids, Andreasson for collisionless matter in GR.

notable.summary: Argue from the vector/one-form distinction why calling a flux across constant-x surfaces a flux 'in the x direction' is misleading.
notable.why_notable: Directly targets the key geometric idea of §4.3 and a common verbal habit.

notable.summary: Show that an arbitrary observer measures dust number density equal to minus the dot product of N with that observer's four-velocity.
notable.why_notable: Gives the frame-free recipe for 'what an observer measures', reused throughout GR.

notable.summary: Recast the first-law relation among rho, n, T and S as a relation between one-forms and show the heat one-form is not the gradient of any function.
notable.why_notable: Connects the thermodynamic idea of heat as a path-dependent quantity to non-exact one-forms.

notable.summary: Explain why, although U^i vanishes in the MCRF, its derivatives cannot be set to zero.
notable.why_notable: Isolates the most frequent logical slip in the Euler-equation derivation.

notable.summary: Modify the particle and energy-momentum conservation laws to include local particle creation and an external four-force, and interpret the force components in the MCRF.
notable.why_notable: Shows what the divergence measures and prepares for coupling matter to fields.

notable.summary: Compute stress-energy components for a uniform particle beam, a thin rotating ring of particles, and two counter-rotating rings.
notable.why_notable: Counter-rotating rings show that zero net momentum does not mean zero stress, a precursor of pressure from random motion.

notable.summary: For a collisionless gas with isotropic velocities in the MCRF, prove the stress-energy tensor is a perfect fluid, express p and rho for particles of one speed, and show radiation has p = rho/3.
notable.why_notable: Makes the 'pressure is momentum flux' aside quantitative and yields the radiation equation of state used in cosmology.

notable.summary: From T^{mn}_{,n} = 0 for a bounded system derive global energy-momentum conservation, the tensor virial theorem, and a higher-moment identity.
notable.why_notable: The tensor virial theorem is the engine behind the quadrupole formula for gravitational radiation later in the book.

notable.summary: Build the stress-energy tensor of starlight in the star's frame, write it in frame-invariant form using the null emission-reception vector, and find how the flux measured by a receding observer depends on speed.
notable.why_notable: A realistic observational application of T and of the 'match in one frame' strategy.

notable.summary: In a long multi-part problem, assemble E and B into the antisymmetric Faraday tensor, check its rotation and boost behaviour, write Maxwell's equations as tensor equations, derive charge conservation, and recover the electric Gauss law from the 4D divergence theorem.
notable.why_notable: The most complete worked-by-reader illustration of the chapter's ideas (current four-vector, conservation, hypersurface integrals) in a second field theory.

difficulty.notes: The early sections (dust, flux, one-forms as surfaces) are gentle and picture based. Difficulty rises in §4.5 (integrating-factor definition of T and S, torque proof) and especially §4.7, the first genuine tensor-calculus manipulation, where learners must track product rules, contractions and MCRF simplifications. Several steps are stated tersely ('it can be shown', 'a little algebra'), there are two printed typos in formulas (Eqs. 4.21, 4.56) and one in the inertia scaling, and §4.8 is qualitative. Readers who skipped Chapter 3's one-form material will struggle with §4.3; readers weak in thermodynamics will find §4.5 abrupt.

cross_references.reason: Lorentz contraction and the gamma factor used to transform densities and fluxes.
Momentarily comoving reference frame of a particle, extended to each fluid element.
Four-velocity components, four-momentum, and E = -p.U (Eq. 2.35) compared with E = <dt, p>.
One-forms, gradients, tensors as multilinear maps, outer products and index raising/lowering are the language used to define N, n~ and T.
Curvature is announced as the next topic; Chapter 5 reuses the MCRF idea as an analogy for local inertial frames.
Conservation law T^{ab}_{,b} = 0 and perfect-fluid equations are carried into curved spacetime with covariant derivatives.
The full stress-energy tensor becomes the source in Einstein's field equations, as §4.8 anticipates.
The tensor virial theorem of Exercise 4.23 underlies the quadrupole formula for gravitational-wave generation.
Relativistic stars: hydrostatic equilibrium with rho + p and pressure as a source, and the limit beyond which no equilibrium exists.
Explicitly cited for black-hole formation and evaporation not conserving baryon number.
Cosmological models use perfect fluids, with dust and radiation (p = rho/3, Exercise 4.22) as limiting equations of state.
Recommended background for the first law, temperature and entropy.
Recommended background in fluid dynamics, including relativistic fluids.

teaching_gems.gem: Count gamma factors to find a tensor's rank: density of a boosted box gains one gamma (vector component), energy density gains two (component of a second-rank tensor).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Turns an abstract rank question into a concrete Lorentz-contraction calculation learners can do in their heads.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Gamma counter: pick a quantity (count, number density, energy density, pressure), boost with a slider, and watch stacked gamma tokens appear, each labelled by its physical origin.

teaching_gems.gem: Density is just a flux across a surface of constant time: world lines piercing a 'now' slice.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Unifies density and flux pictorially before any algebra and makes N = nU feel inevitable.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Rotatable 3D spacetime with a world-line bundle and a movable hypersurface patch that counts piercings, switching between t = const and x = const sheets.

teaching_gems.gem: To decide how many slots a physical quantity needs, ask how many choices you must make: which component of momentum, and which surface it crosses.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives learners a reusable test for whether a quantity is a scalar, vector or (2 0) tensor, and explains the meaning of each T^{ab} at once.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Interactive 4x4 grid of T^{ab}: choose a momentum component (row) and a surface (column) and see an animation of that momentum crossing that surface, with the name of the block.

teaching_gems.gem: Symmetry of stress proved by imagining ever-smaller elements spinning ever faster.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A vivid reductio using only torque and moment-of-inertia scaling; memorable and general (solids too).
teaching_gems.app_idea: Shrinking-cube spin simulator with adjustable T^{xy} and T^{yx}, plotting angular acceleration versus size.

teaching_gems.gem: Write the answer in the rest frame, then find the tensor expression that reproduces it: diag(rho,p,p,p) -> (rho+p)U^aU^b + p eta^{ab}.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Models the standard GR workflow of 'compute where it is easy, promote by covariance', and gives a quick self-check (the 00 entry).
teaching_gems.app_idea: Matrix playground: learner types a candidate covariant expression; the app evaluates it in the MCRF and in boosted frames against the known components.

teaching_gems.gem: Pressure is momentum flux, so even a collisionless gas has pressure; dust is the only pressureless fluid.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Corrects the collision-based picture of pressure and links fluids to kinetic theory and radiation.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Particle gas in a box with collisions toggled off; a counting plane tallies momentum carried across per unit time and area, matching p.

teaching_gems.gem: Split the single equation T^{ab}_{,b} = 0 along and perpendicular to U: the parallel part is the first law (entropy carried unchanged), the perpendicular part is Euler's F = ma with inertia rho + p.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Shows how one tensor equation packages thermodynamics and dynamics, and makes rho + p memorable as inertia.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Projection visualizer: a four-vector equation drawn as an arrow in a (t, x) diagram with the element's U; drag U and see the parallel (energy) and orthogonal (momentum) projections update with their physical labels.

teaching_gems.gem: Pressure feeds gravity in GR, so beyond some compactness adding pressure is self-defeating.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Delivers a striking physical consequence of T as source using only the Euler equation, motivating later stellar-structure chapters.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Compactness slider with an iterative 'pressure needed -> extra gravity -> pressure needed' loop that converges or blows up.

teaching_gems.gem: Conservation via a spacetime box: amount inside at t_2 minus at t_1 equals net inflow through the walls, with outward normals +-dt and +-dx.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Makes the 4D Gauss theorem concrete and explains the sign of the past-face normal.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Draggable spacetime rectangle with world lines; boundary crossings tagged +1/-1 and summed.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed typo in Eq. 4.21: the momentum-density component is printed as rho v^i (1 - v^2) instead of rho v^i/(1 - v^2).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Breaks the visible symmetry T^{0i} = T^{i0} that the text immediately points out, confusing careful readers.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Show the corrected component and let learners verify symmetry from rho U^aU^b.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed typo in Eq. 4.56: the Newtonian acceleration is printed as v-dot + (a.grad)a; it should be v-dot + (v.grad)v, as Exercise 4.17 correctly states.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers unfamiliar with fluid dynamics may learn a wrong advective derivative.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use the corrected expression and connect it to the four-acceleration U^mu_{,b}U^b in the slow-motion limit.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The moment of inertia in the torque argument is written I = alpha rho l^2 ('mass times l^2'), but the mass of the element is rho l^3, so I scales as rho l^5; Eq. 4.28 is correct only with the l^5 scaling.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A reader checking dimensions finds the argument inconsistent and may doubt the conclusion.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present the scaling explicitly: torque ~ l^3, inertia ~ l^5, angular acceleration ~ 1/l^2.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: T is defined through components in an arbitrary frame and its tensor character is deferred to Exercise 4.5; linearity in both arguments is not obvious from the verbal definition.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may feel the definition is circular or that 'flux of momentum' could fail to transform properly.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Pair the definition with the dust construction p(x)N as a concrete tensor, then generalize by linearity over particle species and random velocities.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The integrating-factor step (existence of A, B with drho - (rho+p)dn/n = A dB) and the identification of A/n and B with thermodynamic temperature and entropy are asserted without proof.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Students without thermodynamics background may feel T and S come from nowhere.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Explain that any differential form in two variables has integrating factors (curves of B = const are integral curves), and illustrate with an ideal gas where T and S are known.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: T^{0i} = T^{i0} is justified by the slogan that energy and mass are the same; the argument is heuristic and hides subtleties (e.g. canonical versus symmetrized tensors for fields with spin).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Advanced learners may wonder why some field-theory stress tensors are not symmetric.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Mention that angular-momentum conservation requires a symmetric T and that field theories symmetrize (Belinfante); for fluids the physical argument suffices.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Orientation subtleties of normals in Lorentzian signature are glossed: the one-form dt raised with eta gives a past-pointing vector, and the claim that the 4D Gauss proof is exactly as in 3D hides sign conventions for spacelike boundary pieces.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners who raise indices to draw normal vectors can get signs wrong in flux integrals.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Keep normals as one-forms (as the book does) and demonstrate on the coordinate box that +-dt and +-dx give the right bookkeeping; only then discuss vector normals.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: §4.8 speaks of the acceleration an element 'would have in the absence of pressure' due to the gravitational field, although gravity has not been included in SR fluid dynamics.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers may think gravity simply enters as an external a_i in the SR equations.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Present §4.8 as a heuristic preview and point to the TOV equation derived later for the precise statement.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The claim that p << rho in ordinary situations ('we saw earlier') is given without numbers, and the c = 1 units hide how extreme the ratio is.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners lack intuition for when relativistic pressure corrections matter.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Give SI estimates of p/(rho c^2) for water, the Sun's core, white dwarfs and neutron stars.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The first definition of dust (all particles at rest in one Lorentz frame) is global, while later use is element by element with varying MCRFs.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think dust must be uniformly moving and cannot flow or collapse.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Redefine dust locally: zero velocity dispersion at each event, with a velocity field that can vary.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Heat conduction and viscosity in relativity are dismissed to the bibliography without noting that naive (Eckart-type) relativistic heat-conduction theories violate causality.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Curious learners may try to add Newtonian-style dissipation terms and hit inconsistencies.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add a short note on why dissipative relativistic hydrodynamics needs second-order (Israel-Stewart) theories, with pointers to modern applications such as neutron-star mergers.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'If you run past a cloud of dust, does it look denser, thinner, or the same?' Then 'and how much more energy per cubic metre?' The two answers (one gamma, two gammas) set up N and T.

Order of explanation that works: continuum and MCRF -> dust density and flux -> N = nU and n = sqrt(-N.N) -> world lines through hypersurfaces -> one-forms as surfaces and flux = <n~, N> -> energy density and the one-form counting argument -> T^{ab} dictionary -> dust T -> symmetry -> conservation -> perfect fluid -> projections -> GR preview -> Gauss.
